dataset.name: Java Core Fundamentals
dataset.description: Starter set covering OOP, collections, and exceptions. Expand this file (or add new datasets) to reach the 100-150 question target from docs/07-Question-and-Dataset-Specification.md section 11.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to inherit a class in Java?
questions.explanation: The extends keyword is used when one class inherits from another.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to implement an interface in Java?
questions.explanation: A class uses implements to fulfil the contract defined by an interface.

questions.question: A Java class can extend more than one class at the same time.
questions.explanation: Java supports only single class inheritance. Multiple inheritance of type is achieved through interfaces instead.

questions.question: What is the term for a class that cannot be instantiated directly?
questions.explanation: An abstract class can define behavior and structure for subclasses but cannot itself be instantiated with new.

questions.question: The ______ keyword prevents a method from being overridden in a subclass.
questions.explanation: Marking a method final locks its implementation so subclasses cannot override it.

questions.question: Which of these best describes polymorphism?
options: One method name behaving differently depending on the object it's called on
Hiding internal implementation details from the caller
Bundling data and methods that operate on that data together
Reusing code from a parent class in a child class
questions.answer: One method name behaving differently depending on the object it's called on
questions.explanation: Polymorphism lets the same method call resolve to different behavior depending on the runtime type of the object.

questions.question: Private methods in Java can be overridden by a subclass.
questions.explanation: Private methods are not inherited at all, so a subclass cannot override them - it can only define an unrelated method with the same name.

questions.question: Which interface represents a collection that does not allow duplicate elements?
questions.explanation: Set is specifically defined to disallow duplicate elements, unlike List which permits them.

questions.question: Which class provides a resizable array implementation of the List interface?
questions.explanation: ArrayList backs the List interface with a resizable array, giving fast random access.

questions.question: A HashMap guarantees the iteration order of its entries matches insertion order.
questions.explanation: HashMap makes no ordering guarantee. LinkedHashMap is the variant that preserves insertion order.

questions.question: Which Map implementation keeps its keys sorted?
questions.explanation: TreeMap stores entries in a red-black tree ordered by key, so iteration returns keys in sorted order.

questions.question: The ______ interface represents a collection designed for holding elements prior to processing, typically in FIFO order.
questions.explanation: Queue models a first-in-first-out (or priority-based) collection, commonly implemented by LinkedList or ArrayDeque.

questions.question: What happens if you modify a List while iterating over it with a for-each loop, without using the iterator's own remove method?
options: It silently skips the modified element
It compiles but does nothing at runtime
questions.explanation: Most List implementations fail-fast: structurally modifying the list outside the iterator during iteration throws ConcurrentModificationException.

questions.question: Which block always executes, whether or not an exception is thrown?
questions.explanation: The finally block runs regardless of whether the try block completed normally or threw an exception.

questions.question: RuntimeException and its subclasses are checked exceptions.
questions.explanation: RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked - the compiler does not force you to catch or declare them.

questions.question: Which exception is thrown when you try to access an array index that doesn't exist?
questions.explanation: Accessing an out-of-range array index at runtime throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

questions.question: The keyword used to manually raise an exception in Java is ______.
questions.explanation: throw is used to explicitly raise an exception instance at a specific point in code.

questions.question: If a finally block contains a return statement, what happens to an exception thrown earlier in the try block?
options: The exception propagates normally after finally finishes
The exception is suppressed and the finally block's return value is used instead
The program throws a compile-time error
The exception and the return both propagate together
questions.answer: The exception is suppressed and the finally block's return value is used instead
questions.explanation: A return in finally swallows any exception (or return) from the try/catch block - a classic Java gotcha worth avoiding.

questions.question: String objects in Java are immutable.
questions.explanation: Once created, a String's internal character data cannot change - operations like concat() return a new String instead.

questions.question: Which class should you use for efficient, repeated string concatenation in a loop?
questions.explanation: StringBuilder is mutable and avoids creating a new String object on every concatenation, making it far more efficient in loops. (StringBuffer works too but adds unnecessary synchronization overhead for single-threaded use.)

questions.question: The method used to compare the actual contents of two Strings (not their references) is ______.
questions.explanation: == compares references; equals() compares the actual character content.
